text: "Rosa said my name." I almost shouted hers. The officer covered the radio speaker with his hand. "Above us, something scraped along the pavement." A shoe dragged, stopped, dragged again. I held the button close to my mouth. "I'm here." "For a moment, I heard nothing but her breathing." Then she said, "Stay below the road. I'll get you across."

text: Ross. The canal separated us from a row of dark buildings. Somewhere among them, Rosa was sitting beside a microphone. I searched every window until the officer pulled me back beneath the concrete embankment. Finding her voice hadn't made the street any safer. The maintenance worker could barely put weight on his injured leg. The older woman had taken his bag, but every few steps we still had to stop. Rosa guided us toward a pumping station beneath the road.

text: On the far bank, the older woman and Rosa were helping the worker through an open service entrance. Rosa. No glass between us now. No static. She held the door while we climbed the last steps. The officer pulled its shut. And Rosa dropped a steel bar into its brackets. For a few seconds, all five of us stood in the little entrance chamber, listening. Then she put her arms around me. I had imagined asking her a hundred questions. I couldn't remember any of them.

text: "Correct," she released it. We waited. Across the canal, the man carrying the child stopped beside a car. Someone behind him pointed away from the bridge. Rosa began the warning again. A second voice cut across hers. Canal station, stop transmitting. Her finger lifted from the button. The officer moved closer. The voice returned. Leave the evacuation message alone. Rosa checked the receiver settings. Then she checked them again.
